Apache Tribes - Interceptors
A Tribes channel uses a chain of interceptors between the application-facing GroupChannel and the transport and membership components. An interceptor can transform a message, change how it is delivered, observe traffic, or filter membership events. This keeps each concern independent of the channel and transport implementations.
Interceptors are added with nested Interceptor elements in the order in which they should process outbound messages. Inbound messages and membership events travel through the same chain in reverse order. For the following stack, outbound messages pass through A, then B, while inbound messages pass through B, then A:
<Channel className="org.apache.catalina.tribes.group.GroupChannel"> <Interceptor className="example.A"/> <Interceptor className="example.B"/> </Channel>
An interceptor normally calls the next interceptor when sending and the previous interceptor when receiving. It may instead consume a message, create additional messages, delay delivery, or report an error. Therefore, both the selected interceptors and their order are part of the cluster protocol and should be consistent on every member.
A channel message carries a bit mask of send options. An interceptor with an optionFlag of zero processes every message. A non-zero flag allows the interceptor to process only messages that contain all of its configured bits. Some interceptors use a fixed or internal option bit. For example, MessageDispatchInterceptor reacts to SEND_OPTIONS_ASYNCHRONOUS, while GzipInterceptor marks compressed messages so that the receiver knows to decompress them.
Custom option bits must not overlap. Set optionCheck="true" on the channel during configuration to make startup fail when two interceptors claim the same non-zero flag. The standard delivery options are described in the transport guide.
MessageDispatchInterceptor queues messages marked with SEND_OPTIONS_ASYNCHRONOUS and sends them from its worker pool. A queue size limit bounds the retained message data. When the queue is full, alwaysSend determines whether the caller sends the message synchronously or receives an error.
Its position controls which outbound work is asynchronous. Interceptors before it run on the caller's thread; interceptors after it run on a dispatch worker. If no interceptors are configured, GroupChannel adds this interceptor automatically. Once an explicit stack is configured, include it explicitly when asynchronous delivery is required.
FragmentationInterceptor splits messages larger than maxSize and reassembles the fragments at the destination. Incomplete fragment sets are discarded after expire. This can prevent one large message from monopolising a connection, but it also retains fragments in memory until the message is complete or expires.
GzipInterceptor compresses outbound payloads with GZIP when they exceed compressionMinSize and decompresses marked inbound payloads. Compression reduces network traffic for suitable data at the cost of CPU time. Place it before FragmentationInterceptor to compress a complete message before splitting it; the reverse inbound path then reassembles the message before decompression.
OrderInterceptor adds a sequence number per destination and queues out-of-order inbound messages. The expire, maxQueue and forwardExpired settings bound how long and how many messages it retains, and determine whether gaps result in late messages being forwarded or discarded. Ordering can reduce throughput when many threads send concurrently, so enable it only for messages whose semantics require it.
TwoPhaseCommitInterceptor sends a confirmation after each message. The receiver releases the original only after the confirmation arrives. It does not retransmit a lost message or confirmation, so it is a delivery-ordering mechanism rather than a transaction manager.
When it is combined with FragmentationInterceptor, declare TwoPhaseCommitInterceptor first. This makes it confirm the complete message rather than individual fragments that share the same message identifier.
TcpFailureDetector checks a member over TCP before accepting a disappearance event, and also reacts to message send failures. It helps distinguish an unavailable member from delayed or lost membership announcements. Connection and optional read tests have independent timeouts so that failure confirmation can be tuned for the network.
TcpPingInterceptor actively sends periodic pings. It may use the channel heartbeat or a dedicated thread, and it can limit checks to statically configured members. Place it before TcpFailureDetector so it can use the detector's membership checks.
StaticMembershipInterceptor adds configured local and remote members to the view without requiring dynamic discovery. It may be used alone or with a dynamic membership service. Place it after TcpFailureDetector so the configured members receive the same failure checks as dynamically discovered members. The membership guide contains complete examples and ordering guidance.
DomainFilterInterceptor exposes only members and messages whose member domain matches its configured domain. It provides logical separation when discovery traffic is shared. It is not a security boundary: untrusted cluster traffic still requires the network and TLS protections described in the cluster security reference.
SimpleCoordinator derives a stable, sorted member view and selects its first member as coordinator. NonBlockingCoordinator adds a distributed view-merging and leader-election protocol. These are specialised building blocks for applications using Tribes directly and are not normally required for Tomcat session replication.
ThroughputInterceptor counts transmitted and received messages, bytes and send failures, and periodically logs transfer rates. It does not change message delivery. The interceptor and several other built-ins expose runtime state through JMX when channel JMX registration is enabled. See the status and monitoring guide for object names and useful attributes.
The channel also invokes heartbeat() periodically. Interceptors use this callback to expire fragments, ordering queues, confirmations and other temporary state. If the channel's internal heartbeat is disabled, the embedding application or container must provide the equivalent periodic callback.
The following stack checks member failures, permits asynchronous sends, compresses larger messages and fragments the compressed representation. Each cluster member should use the same message-processing stack and compatible settings.
<Channel className="org.apache.catalina.tribes.group.GroupChannel" optionCheck="true"> <Interceptor className="org.apache.catalina.tribes.group.interceptors.TcpFailureDetector"/> <Interceptor className="org.apache.catalina.tribes.group.interceptors.MessageDispatchInterceptor" maxQueueSize="67108864"/> <Interceptor className="org.apache.catalina.tribes.group.interceptors.GzipInterceptor" compressionMinSize="4096"/> <Interceptor className="org.apache.catalina.tribes.group.interceptors.FragmentationInterceptor" maxSize="102400"/> </Channel>
The interceptor configuration reference lists the supported attributes and defaults for interceptors intended for Tomcat cluster configurations. The interceptor package API covers the specialised implementations.
Custom interceptors should extend ChannelInterceptorBase and override only the callbacks they need. Outbound processing must normally finish by calling super.sendMessage(); inbound processing and membership notifications must normally finish by calling the corresponding superclass method. Omitting that call intentionally consumes the event.
A single interceptor instance is shared by sending threads, receiver worker threads and heartbeat processing. Mutable state must therefore be safe for concurrent access, callbacks should avoid blocking the stack unnecessarily, and retained messages must be cloned if their buffers may be reused by the caller. Release temporary state during heartbeat or shutdown, and use an application-specific, non-conflicting bit when the interceptor needs an optionFlag.
